title: My arm keeps giving out: intermittent right arm weakness in a 63-year-old electrician in general practice
desc: This station involves a focused history and a structured neurological examination of the upper limbs in John Pascoe, a 63-year-old electrician seen in general practice. For 6 weeks his right arm has given out every now and then when he lifts or reaches overhead. He also has right neck pain that runs down his arm to his thumb. The candidate examines inspection, tone, power, reflexes and coordination, and screens for upper motor neuron signs. In Part 2 they interpret his observations, blood tests and MRI cervical spine report. They diagnose a right C5 and C6 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis, contrast upper and lower motor neuron signs, and plan analgesia, physiotherapy, referral to a spinal surgeon and safety netting for spinal cord compression and stroke.
focus: Performing a structured upper limb neurological examination, telling a lower motor neuron root lesion from an upper motor neuron one, and managing cervical radiculopathy in general practice
diagnosis: Cervical spondylosis with right foraminal stenosis
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. John Pascoe, a 63-year-old man, has come to see the GP because his arm has been weak at times. Your GP supervisor has asked you to assess him first, including a neurological examination of his upper limbs.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Pascoe and perform a focused neurological examination of the upper limbs, telling the examiner what you are examining, then summarise your findings (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Pascoe's observations, his blood results and his MRI cervical spine report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are John Pascoe, a 63-year-old electrician. You are right-handed. You are friendly and practical, but worried. You hold your neck a little stiffly and move your head carefully. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “My right arm keeps giving out on me every now and then.”

The weakness (give only when asked):

  • What happens: when you lift something up to a high shelf, or hold your arm up or out (for example, holding a drill up to the ceiling), the arm “just gives out” and you have to drop it down. It comes back after you rest it for a few minutes. Bending the elbow to carry things also feels weaker than it used to.
  • How often: a few times a week, always when you are using the arm.
  • When it started: about 6 weeks ago. You spent a weekend fitting downlights in your daughter's house, looking up at the ceiling for hours. Your neck was stiff and sore on the right the next morning, and within a few days the pain was shooting down your arm.
  • Course: about the same for the last month. It is not getting worse.
  • Hand: your grip is fine. You can do up buttons, write and use your tools without fumbling.
  • Has it ever come on suddenly, out of the blue? No. It only happens when you are lifting or reaching.

Pain and other feelings (give only when asked):

  • Where: the right side of your neck, over your right shoulder blade and the top of your shoulder, then down the outside of your upper arm and forearm into your thumb.
  • What it feels like: a deep ache with a burning streak down the arm. About 4/10 now, and up to 7/10 at night or after a work day.
  • Pins and needles: yes, in your right thumb and index finger, on and off.
  • Worse with: looking up, turning your head to the right, and long days at work.
  • Better with: resting your right hand on top of your head (“funny, but it helps”), and paracetamol and ibuprofen, which take the edge off.
  • Night: it wakes you if you lie on that side, but it settles when you change position.

Say no if asked about:

  • sudden weakness or numbness of your face, arm or leg that came out of the blue; a drooping face; slurred speech or trouble finding words; loss of vision or double vision;
  • symptoms in your left arm or in either leg; clumsy hands, dropping things, trouble with buttons or handwriting; unsteadiness or a change in your walking;
  • trouble passing urine, leaking, or any change in your bowels; an electric shock down your spine when you bend your neck;
  • a fall, a car accident or any injury to your neck;
  • fever, sweats, weight loss, a cough or coughing up blood, a history of cancer, or steroid medicines;
  • your shoulder catching or locking, or a painful shoulder injury;
  • twitching of the muscles.

Past medical history: high blood pressure for 8 years and high cholesterol. Left knee arthroscopy in 2015. No diabetes, heart problems or strokes.

Medicines: perindopril 5 mg in the morning and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. For the last 6 weeks you have taken paracetamol 1 g up to three times a day, and for 2 weeks ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a week.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your father had a stroke at 74 and died at 80. Your mother had arthritis.

Social history:

  • Work: electrician, now working 3 days a week. A lot of it is overhead work on ladders. You drive your work ute.
  • Smoking: you smoked a pack a day from 18 and quit 10 years ago, at 53.
  • Alcohol: 2 beers most nights.
  • Home: you live with your wife, Margaret. You are independent.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: “I wondered if I'd pinched a nerve, or done something to my shoulder.”
  • Concern (say this when asked what worries you): “Dad had a stroke. I'm worried this is how it started for him.”
  • Expectation: you want to know what is wrong, to get it fixed, and to keep working.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Is this a stroke coming on?” Accept a brief answer, or a promise to come back to it once the tests are done.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • Before starting (if asked about pain): “My neck's sore, and the right arm aches.” He is seated in a chair, fully dressed.
  • General inspection: alert, comfortable at rest, holds his neck stiffly. No scars or deformity. Mild wasting of the right deltoid and biceps compared with the left. No fasciculations. Shoulder contour otherwise symmetrical.
  • Cervical spine: mild tenderness over the right lower cervical paraspinal muscles. Extension and right rotation are reduced and bring on pain down the right arm to the thumb. Flexion and left rotation are full. Spurling's test on the right (if performed): reproduces the pain into the right arm and thumb.
  • Tone: normal in both arms at the elbow and wrist. No catch on rapid pronation and supination. No rigidity.
  • Pronator drift: none on either side.
  • Power (MRC):
    • Right shoulder abduction 4/5. Right elbow flexion 4/5. Right wrist extension 4+/5.
    • Right shoulder adduction, elbow extension, wrist flexion, finger extension, finger flexion, finger abduction and adduction, and thumb abduction: all 5/5.
    • Left arm: 5/5 in every movement.
    • Effort is good, and pain does not limit testing.
  • Reflexes: right biceps and brachioradialis reduced, and still reduced with reinforcement. Left biceps and brachioradialis normal. Triceps and finger jerks normal and equal on both sides. Tapping the brachioradialis does not cause finger flexion. Hoffmann's sign (if tested) is negative on both sides.
  • Coordination: finger-nose testing is accurate on both sides. Rapid alternating movements are normal on both sides.
  • Sensation: if the candidate says they would examine sensation, say: “You do not need to examine sensation today. Assume pinprick and light touch are reduced over the right lateral forearm, thumb and index finger, and are otherwise normal.”
  • Shoulder (if examined): full passive range of movement. No painful arc. No tenderness.
  • Lower limbs and gait (if the candidate offers to check them): normal tone, power and reflexes. No clonus. Plantars flexor. Gait normal, including heel-to-toe walking.
  • Observations (if asked): taken by the practice nurse: BP 136/84 mmHg, HR 72/min regular, temperature 36.6 °C. The full set is handed over in Part 2.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Mr Pascoe's identity, explains the examination and gains consent.
Asks about pain before touching him, exposes both arms, shoulders and the neck, and positions him sitting on the edge of the bed with his forearms resting on a pillow.
Acknowledges his fear of a stroke and his worry about work, gives clear instructions during the examination (demonstrating movements), and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the weakness:

kids.x: Pattern: the right arm gives out when lifting or reaching overhead and when carrying with the elbow bent, recovers after rest; grip and fine hand use are normal.
Onset and course: began 6 weeks ago after a weekend of overhead ceiling work; a few times a week; stable for the last month, not getting worse.
kids.d: Award only if the candidate asks whether it is getting worse.

check.x: Characterises the pain and sensory symptoms: right neck pain radiating over the shoulder and down the lateral arm and forearm to the thumb, with pins and needles in the thumb and index finger; worse looking up and turning to the right, eased by resting the hand on his head; wakes him on that side.
check.d: Award if the distribution of the pain and the paraesthesia are both established.

check.x: Screens for TIA or stroke: sudden-onset weakness or numbness, facial droop, speech or vision disturbance, leg involvement [none; the weakness only comes with use].
Screens for spinal cord compression: clumsy hands (buttons, handwriting), symptoms in the other arm or legs, unsteady gait, bladder or bowel change, Lhermitte's phenomenon [none].
check.d: Award for at least three of these.

check.x: Screens for red flags of serious spinal disease (trauma, fever, weight loss or sweats, cancer history, steroid use or immunosuppression), and shoulder injury or locking, muscle twitching [none].
check.d: Award for at least three of the spinal red flags.

check.x: Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history: hypertension and high cholesterol, knee arthroscopy; perindopril 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg; paracetamol and ibuprofen for 6 and 2 weeks; no allergies.

Takes a social, family and vascular risk history: right-handed electrician doing overhead work on ladders, drives a work ute; ex-smoker (about 35 pack-years, quit 10 years ago); 2 beers most nights; lives with his wife; father had a stroke at 74.
check.d: Award if handedness, occupation, smoking and the family history of stroke are established.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders about a pinched nerve or his shoulder, fears a stroke like his father's, wants it fixed and to keep working.
Examination
Inspects both arms and the shoulder girdle for posture, scars, deformity, muscle bulk and fasciculations, comparing sides [mild wasting of the right deltoid and biceps; no fasciculations].
Inspects and examines the cervical spine: tenderness and range of movement [extension and right rotation reduced and reproduce the right arm pain].
check.d: Spurling's test is not required, but credit it here if performed.

check.x: Assesses tone with him relaxed: passive flexion and extension at the elbow and wrist with the elbow supported, and rapid pronation and supination [normal on both sides, no catch].
Tests for pronator drift with the arms outstretched, palms up and eyes closed [none].
Tests power:

kids.x: Shoulder abduction and adduction, elbow flexion and extension, and wrist extension and flexion on both sides.
Finger extension, flexion, abduction and adduction, and thumb abduction on both sides.
kids.d: Award if the finger and thumb movements are tested on both sides; the individual movements need not all be named.

kids.x: Technique: isolates each movement by stabilising the joint above, compares each movement side to side, and grades it on the MRC scale.
Finds weakness of right shoulder abduction (4/5), elbow flexion (4/5) and wrist extension (4+/5), with the rest of both arms 5/5.

check.x: Tests reflexes:

kids.x: Technique: arms relaxed, compares sides, and uses reinforcement when a reflex is reduced.

Tests the biceps, brachioradialis, triceps and finger jerks and finds the right biceps and brachioradialis reduced (even with reinforcement), the triceps and finger jerks normal, and no inverted supinator reflex.
kids.d: Award if biceps, brachioradialis and triceps are tested on both sides and the reduced right biceps and brachioradialis are identified; finger jerks are desirable but not required.

check.x: Looks for upper motor neuron signs of cord involvement: Hoffmann's sign, and offers to examine the lower limbs and gait (tone, reflexes, clonus, plantars) [all normal].
check.d: Award if Hoffmann's sign is tested or the lower limb examination is offered.

check.x: Tests coordination: finger-nose and rapid alternating movements on both sides [normal].
States they would test sensation by dermatome (pinprick and/or light touch), and identifies the examiner's finding (right lateral forearm, thumb and index finger) as the C6 dermatome.
check.d: Do not require temperature, vibration or proprioception to be named; the examiner stops the candidate at this step.

check.x: Summarises the examination: a lower motor neuron pattern in the right C5 and C6 distribution (weakness, wasting, reduced reflexes, normal tone), with no upper motor neuron signs.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations as normal: BP 136/84 then 132/82 on treatment, a regular pulse (no atrial fibrillation at the time of assessment), afebrile.

Interprets the bloods as normal: normal FBC, CRP and ESR (no sign of infection, inflammation or malignancy), HbA1c 5.6% (below the diabetic threshold, so diabetes is an unlikely cause of a neuropathy), and normal kidney function (a short NSAID course is possible with care alongside perindopril).
check.d: Award if the inflammatory markers and at least one other result are interpreted.

check.x: Interprets the MRI: severe right C5-6 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C6 root and moderate right C4-5 foraminal stenosis contacting the right C5 root, which matches the clinical levels; normal cord with no compression or signal change; no destructive or infective lesion.
check.d: Award only if the candidate states both the concordant root compression and the normal cord.

check.x: Gives right C5 and C6 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis as the most likely diagnosis, justified by radicular pain and paraesthesia in the C5 to C6 distribution, myotomal weakness, reduced C5 to C6 reflexes, pain reproduced by neck extension and rotation, and concordant MRI findings; credit correct root values for his signs (shoulder abduction C5; elbow flexion and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes C5 to C6; wrist extension C6 to C7).
check.d: Credit correct root values for his signs wherever in Part 2 they are given.

check.x: Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: cervical spondylotic myelopathy, TIA, motor neurone disease, rotator cuff pathology, brachial neuritis.
check.d: Award for at least three, including myelopathy and TIA, each justified.

check.x: Contrasts upper motor neuron signs:

kids.x: Lists them: weakness in a pyramidal pattern, pronator drift, increased tone (spasticity), hyperreflexia, clonus, a positive Hoffmann's sign and upgoing (Babinski) plantars.

Explains why it matters: cord compression at C5-6 gives lower motor neuron signs at that level with upper motor neuron signs below it (inverted supinator reflex, brisk triceps and finger jerks, leg signs), which would need urgent surgical referral.

check.x: Management

Explains in plain language that a nerve in the neck is pinched by wear and tear, that this is not a stroke, that the MRI shows no pressure on the spinal cord, and that most people improve over weeks to months.

Plans analgesia: regular paracetamol, with a short course of an NSAID taken with food if there is no contraindication, noting the caution with perindopril (BP and kidney function); avoids routine opioids.
check.d: Accept the drugs and the caution without exact doses.

check.x: Advises staying active with physiotherapy, and modified duties with no ladders or overhead work and a medical certificate.
Refers to a spinal surgeon (neurosurgery or orthopaedic spine) because of the objective motor weakness with concordant MRI.
Safety netting

Names spinal red flags in plain words, with same-day ED review: the arm weakness getting worse or spreading, weakness or numbness in both arms or in the legs, clumsy hands, unsteady walking, or loss of bladder or bowel control; and arranges a specific planned GP review (1 to 2 weeks).
check.d: Award for at least three red flags with same-day ED, and a specific planned GP review (1 to 2 weeks).

check.x: Names stroke symptoms with 000 (FAST): sudden facial droop, sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, slurred speech or trouble finding words, or sudden loss of vision, even if they settle.

part2.lead: Your GP supervisor saw Mr Pascoe after you and arranged blood tests and an MRI of his cervical spine. He has come back 10 days later to discuss the results; his arm is about the same. Here are the practice nurse's observations from his first visit, his blood results and his MRI report.
part2.patient:
• At the start of the management answer, when the candidate explains the diagnosis to you, ask: “So it's not a stroke, then? Will I need an operation?”
  • During the management answer, ask: “Can I keep working? And what should I be watching out for?” Let the candidate answer: this is where the safety netting is scored.

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, first visit)
handover.result: Taken seated in the treatment room at the first visit, with a repeat BP after 10 minutes' rest.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, HR 72 then 70 and regular, BP 136/84 then 132/82 mmHg, temperature 36.6 °C, alert, pain 4/10. All within normal adult ranges, so no escalation is needed.
  • For Mr Pascoe: his BP is controlled on perindopril and his pulse is regular (no atrial fibrillation at the time of assessment), so nothing here points to an embolic TIA. He is afebrile, which argues against spinal infection.
  • What it changes: he is stable and can be managed in general practice. The BP is a baseline while he continues ibuprofen; recheck it if he keeps using an NSAID with perindopril.

handover.label: Blood tests (taken after the first visit)
handover.result: Collected at the local collection centre, 2 days after the first visit.
handover.model:
• Read: normal full blood count; CRP 3 mg/L and ESR 12 mm/h, both normal; normal sodium, potassium and creatinine, eGFR over 90; HbA1c 5.6%.
  • For Mr Pascoe: normal inflammatory markers and blood count make infection (discitis, epidural abscess) or malignancy unlikely. HbA1c 5.6%, below the 6.5% diagnostic threshold, makes diabetes, and therefore a diabetic neuropathy, an unlikely cause.
  • What it changes: normal kidney function means a short NSAID course is possible, used with care alongside perindopril and with BP rechecked.

handover.label: MRI cervical spine (8 days after the first visit)
handover.result:
Examination: MRI cervical spine without contrast. Sagittal T1, T2 and STIR; axial T2 from C2 to T1.

Clinical details: 63-year-old right-handed man with 6 weeks of right neck pain radiating to the lateral forearm and thumb, with paraesthesia. Weakness of right shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, reduced sensation over the right lateral forearm, thumb and index finger. No upper motor neuron signs. ?Radiculopathy.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Alignment: mild straightening of the normal cervical lordosis. No listhesis.
  • Vertebral bodies: normal height and marrow signal. No fracture, marrow oedema or destructive lesion.
  • Discs: degenerative disc height loss from C4-5 to C6-7.
  • C4-5: disc-osteophyte complex with right uncovertebral hypertrophy. Moderate right foraminal stenosis, contacting the exiting right C5 nerve root. Left foramen patent. Central canal adequate.
  • C5-6: broad disc-osteophyte complex with a right foraminal component and right uncovertebral and facet hypertrophy. Severe right foraminal stenosis, compressing the exiting right C6 nerve root. Mild left foraminal narrowing. Mild central canal narrowing with CSF preserved around the cord.
  • C6-7: mild disc bulge. No canal or foraminal stenosis.
  • Spinal cord: normal calibre and signal throughout. No cord compression and no intramedullary signal change.
  • Craniocervical junction and paravertebral soft tissues: normal. No collection.

Conclusion: multilevel cervical spondylosis with severe right C5-6 and moderate right C4-5 foraminal stenosis, compressing the right C6 nerve root and contacting the right C5 nerve root, concordant with the clinical findings. No spinal cord compression or myelopathic signal change. No destructive or infective lesion.
handover.model:
• Read: degenerative (spondylotic) change from C4-5 to C6-7. At C5-6 the right foramen is severely narrowed and the right C6 root is compressed. At C4-5 the right foramen is moderately narrowed and touches the right C5 root. The canal is only mildly narrowed and the cord is normal, with no signal change. No fracture, tumour or infection.
  • For Mr Pascoe: the levels match the examination: shoulder abduction (C5), elbow flexion and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes (C5 to C6) and wrist extension (C6 to C7, here C6), with the C6 sensory change. This confirms a right C5 and C6 radiculopathy. A normal cord fits the absence of upper motor neuron signs, so there is no myelopathy.
  • What it changes: a root lesion, not a stroke, which answers his fear. An objective motor deficit with concordant compression warrants referral to a spinal surgeon, while conservative care starts now.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of John Pascoe, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Pascoe now, here in general practice.
Which upper motor neuron signs would tell you his spinal cord is involved, and why does that matter?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; John Pascoe, 63, right-handed electrician.
  • Situation: 6 weeks of the right arm giving out with overhead lifting, and right neck pain radiating to the thumb with paraesthesia; back for results.
  • Background: began after overhead ceiling work; hypertension, high cholesterol, ex-smoker of about 35 pack-years, father had a stroke; no stroke, cord or systemic red flags.
  • Assessment: right deltoid and biceps wasting; shoulder abduction and elbow flexion 4/5, wrist extension 4+/5; reduced right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes; normal tone, no Hoffmann's: lower motor neuron, C5 to C6. Normal observations with a regular pulse; normal bloods. MRI: severe right C5-6 and moderate C4-5 foraminal stenosis, normal cord. Right C5 and C6 radiculopathy.
  • Recommendation: analgesia, physiotherapy, modified duties, spinal surgical referral; GP review in 2 weeks.

Most likely: right C5 and C6 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. For: radicular pain and paraesthesia to the thumb; weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension; reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes; pain reproduced by neck extension and rotation; concordant MRI.

  • Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: for: age, multilevel spondylosis. Against: no hand clumsiness, gait or bladder symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, normal cord on MRI.
  • TIA: for: vascular risk factors, father's stroke. Against: weakness only with use, not sudden; fixed root pattern with reduced reflexes and pain.
  • Motor neurone disease: for: weakness and wasting. Against: pain and sensory change, no fasciculations, deficit confined to two roots.
  • Rotator cuff pathology: for: weak shoulder abduction in an overhead worker. Against: full passive shoulder movement with no painful arc, pain and paraesthesia below the elbow to the thumb, elbow flexion weakness and reduced reflexes.
  • Brachial neuritis: for: shoulder girdle weakness and wasting. Against: no preceding acute, severe shoulder pain that then eased as weakness appeared; the pain is mechanical neck pain reproduced by neck extension, rotation and Spurling's test; concordant root compression on MRI.

1. Explain: a pinched nerve in the neck from wear and tear; not a stroke; the spinal cord is not squeezed; most people improve over weeks to months. An operation isn't needed now; the spinal surgeon will advise, and surgery is considered only if weakness persists or worsens or the pain can't be controlled.
  2. Analgesia: regular paracetamol; a short NSAID course with food if there is no contraindication, with care alongside perindopril (recheck BP and kidney function); avoid routine opioids.
  3. Activity and work: stay active, physiotherapy; modified duties with no ladders, overhead work or sustained neck extension; certificate.
  4. Referral: spinal surgeon (neurosurgery or orthopaedic spine) because of the motor deficit.
  5. Safety netting (when he asks): same-day ED for worsening or spreading weakness, symptoms in both arms or the legs, clumsy hands, unsteady walking, or bladder or bowel change; 000 for a sudden facial droop, sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, slurred speech or trouble finding words, or sudden loss of vision, even if it settles; GP review in 2 weeks.

• Upper motor neuron signs to look for: pyramidal weakness, pronator drift, spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus, a positive Hoffmann's sign, and upgoing (Babinski) plantars.
  • Why it matters: cord compression at C5-6 gives lower motor neuron signs at that level and upper motor neuron signs below it (inverted supinator reflex, brisk triceps and finger jerks, leg signs), needing urgent surgical referral. He has none, and his cord is normal on MRI.

ddx.dx: Right C5 and C6 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis (foraminal stenosis)
ddx.for: Right neck pain radiating to the thumb with paraesthesia, weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, pain reproduced by neck extension, and concordant right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis on MRI.

ddx.dx: Rotator cuff tear or shoulder impingement
ddx.for: Weakness of shoulder abduction in a tradesman who does a lot of overhead work.
ddx.against: Full passive shoulder movement with no painful arc, pain and paraesthesia running below the elbow to the thumb, elbow flexion weakness and reduced reflexes.

ddx.for: Shoulder girdle weakness with wasting of the deltoid and biceps.
ddx.against: No acute severe shoulder pain followed by weakness; the pain comes from the neck, is reproduced by neck movement, and the MRI shows concordant root compression.

ddx.for: A 63-year-old with multilevel cervical spondylosis and mild canal narrowing at C5-6.
ddx.against: No hand clumsiness, gait change or bladder symptoms, normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign or inverted supinator reflex, normal lower limbs and a normal cord on MRI.

ddx.for: Episodes of arm weakness in a man with hypertension, high cholesterol, a 35 pack-year smoking history and a father who had a stroke.
ddx.against: The weakness is never sudden in onset; it comes only when he loads the arm and settles with rest, with no face, speech or leg involvement, and there is a fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain.

ddx.for: Arm weakness with muscle wasting at 63.
ddx.against: Pain and sensory symptoms, no fasciculations, no upper motor neuron signs anywhere (normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign, normal lower limbs), a deficit confined to two roots and concordant root compression on MRI.

guide:
Part 1:

  • The history should take about 4 minutes, leaving about 6 minutes for a structured upper limb examination. The structured upper limb examination is the core of this station, so mark the technique as well as the findings.
  • Mr Pascoe starts seated in a chair, fully dressed: the candidate must expose and position him (item 3).
  • Give each finding only when the candidate performs or names that step. Accept a briefly demonstrated technique.
  • If the candidate offers sensation, say they do not need to examine it, and give the C6 sensory finding as written (item 23).
  • If the candidate offers the lower limbs or gait, give the normal findings. Credit item 21 for testing Hoffmann's sign or offering the lower limb examination.
  • Mr Pascoe asks “Is this a stroke coming on?” near the end. A brief, honest answer is enough. It is scored formally in Part 2 (item 33).
  • At 9 minutes, if the candidate has not summarised, say: “Please summarise your examination findings.”

Part 2:

  • Hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order.
  • Score items 26 to 28 from the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer, and items 29 and 30 from the diagnosis answer.
  • Credit correct root values for his signs within item 29 wherever in Part 2 they are given (the ISBAR, the diagnosis answer or the fourth question).
  • Score item 33 from the diagnosis or the management answer, including the reply to his question. Score items 34 to 36 from the management answer. Mr Pascoe asks what to watch out for during it: score the safety-netting items (38 and 39) from that reply.
  • Advice on driving is good practice but is not scored.
  • Score item 31 from the fourth question.

High-performing candidate:

  • Pins down the radicular pain and its trigger, and clearly separates use-related weakness from sudden TIA symptoms.
  • Screens for myelopathy and systemic red flags.
  • Examines in order (inspection, tone, drift, power, reflexes, coordination), isolates and compares each movement, uses reinforcement, and looks for Hoffmann's sign.
  • Summarises a right C5 to C6 lower motor neuron lesion before seeing the MRI.
  • In Part 2, matches the MRI levels to the signs, reassures him honestly that this is not a stroke, plans conservative care with surgical referral for the motor deficit, and gives clear spinal and stroke red flags.

Borderline candidate:

  • Tests power without isolating movements or comparing sides.
  • Omits the brachioradialis or reinforcement, or does not look for upper motor neuron signs.
  • Confuses upper and lower motor neuron signs, or labels it a stroke or a shoulder problem.
  • Gives vague safety netting.
explain:
The upper limb neurological examination

Prepare first: introduce yourself, explain the examination, gain consent, perform hand hygiene and ask about pain. Expose both arms, the shoulders and the neck. Sit the patient on the edge of the bed with the forearms on a pillow. Then work through the steps in order, always comparing sides:

  1. Inspection: posture, scars, deformity, muscle bulk (wasting) and fasciculations, and the cervical spine.
  2. Tone: with the patient relaxed, passively flex and extend the elbow and wrist with the elbow supported, and use rapid pronation and supination to feel for a supinator catch (spasticity).
  3. Pronator drift: arms outstretched, palms up, eyes closed. A drift down and into pronation is a subtle upper motor neuron sign.
  4. Power: shoulder abduction and adduction, elbow flexion and extension, wrist extension and flexion, finger extension, flexion, abduction and adduction, and thumb abduction. Isolate each movement by stabilising the joint above, give clear instructions, and grade on the MRC scale.
  5. Reflexes: biceps, brachioradialis, triceps and finger jerks, with the patient relaxed. Use reinforcement (clenching the teeth) before calling a reflex absent.
  6. Coordination: finger-nose testing and rapid alternating movements.
  7. Sensation: map pinprick and light touch by dermatome, then test temperature, and vibration and proprioception distally (moving proximally if impaired).

MRC grades: 0 no contraction; 1 a flicker; 2 movement with gravity eliminated; 3 movement against gravity; 4 movement against some resistance; 5 normal power.

Root values

Movement or reflexRoot
Shoulder abductionC5 (C5 to C6)
Elbow flexionC5 to C6
Elbow extensionC7 (C6 to C8)
Wrist extensionC6 to C7
Wrist flexionC7 to C8
Finger extensionC7 to C8
Finger flexionC8

Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

  • Upper motor neuron: weakness in a pyramidal pattern (in the arm, extensors weaker than flexors), pronator drift, increased tone (spasticity), hyperreflexia, clonus, a positive Hoffmann's sign and upgoing (Babinski) plantars.
  • Lower motor neuron: weakness in a root or nerve distribution, wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes and flexor plantars.

A lesion of the cervical cord gives lower motor neuron signs at the level of the lesion and upper motor neuron signs below it. The classic example at C5 to C6 is the inverted supinator reflex. Tapping the brachioradialis produces no brachioradialis jerk (lower motor neuron at C5 to C6), but the fingers flex because the reflexes below the level are brisk.

Why Mr Pascoe has a right C5 and C6 radiculopathy

  • History: radicular pain from the neck over the shoulder to the lateral forearm and thumb, with thumb and index paraesthesia. It is worse with neck extension and rotation towards the painful side, which narrow the foramen. It is eased by resting the hand on the head (the shoulder abduction relief sign). It began after hours of overhead work with his neck extended.
  • His “occasional” weakness: the weakness is fixed but mild (4/5). He notices it only when he loads the arm overhead.
  • Examination: a lower motor neuron deficit confined to C5 and C6: weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension; wasting of the deltoid and biceps; reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes; and C6 sensory loss. Triceps, finger flexion and the small hand muscles are spared. There are no upper motor neuron signs.
  • Typical age: spondylotic foraminal stenosis is the usual cause of cervical radiculopathy after middle age.

Differentials that matter

  • Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: the important one to exclude in an older patient with spondylosis. Look for clumsy hands, gait unsteadiness, bladder symptoms, Lhermitte's phenomenon and upper motor neuron signs.
  • TIA: his vascular risk and family history make it worth considering, especially as he fears it. TIA weakness is sudden, maximal at onset, not triggered by loading a particular movement, and usually resolves within an hour. It does not come with radicular pain, wasting or reduced reflexes.
  • Motor neurone disease: causes painless weakness with wasting and fasciculations and a mix of upper and lower motor neuron signs, without sensory loss. Mr Pascoe has pain, sensory change, no fasciculations and no upper motor neuron signs anywhere (normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign, normal lower limbs).
  • Rotator cuff pathology: causes painful weakness of abduction, but the reflexes and sensation are normal and the pain stays above the elbow.
  • Brachial neuritis: severe acute shoulder pain over days, then patchy weakness and wasting as the pain settles.

The results

  • Observations: normal, with a regular pulse.
  • Bloods: normal inflammatory markers and blood count, so infection or malignancy is unlikely. HbA1c is below the 6.5% diagnostic threshold, so diabetes is an unlikely cause. Normal kidney function.
  • MRI: right foraminal stenosis at the clinically affected levels, with a normal cord. Imaging is indicated here because there is an objective motor deficit. MRI findings must always be matched to the clinical picture, because degenerative changes are common in people without symptoms.

Management

  • Explanation: most cervical radiculopathy improves with conservative care over weeks to months.
  • Analgesia: simple analgesia, with a short NSAID course if appropriate. NSAIDs need care with an ACE inhibitor: check BP and kidney function.
  • Alcohol: brief alcohol advice (no more than 10 standard drinks a week); alcohol adds to the stomach-bleeding risk of NSAIDs.
  • Activity: stay active, physiotherapy, and modify work to avoid sustained neck extension and overhead tasks.
  • Referral: a definite motor deficit warrants referral to a spinal surgeon. A nerve root injection, or decompression (anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, or foraminotomy), is considered when weakness persists or progresses or pain stays uncontrolled.
  • Urgency: progressive or severe weakness, or any sign of myelopathy, needs urgent surgical assessment.

Safety netting

  • Same-day ED: weakness that worsens or spreads, symptoms in both arms or the legs, clumsy hands, unsteady walking, or a change in bladder or bowel control. These suggest cord compression.
  • Call 000: a sudden facial droop, slurred speech or trouble finding words, sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, or sudden loss of vision, even if it goes away. These suggest a stroke.
  • Follow-up: GP review in about 2 weeks to recheck power and reflexes, with the physiotherapy and surgical appointments.
points: Examine the upper limbs in a fixed order, comparing sides at every step: inspection, tone, pronator drift, power, reflexes, coordination, then sensation. Isolate each movement and use reinforcement before calling a reflex absent.

Lower motor neuron signs are weakness in a root or nerve pattern, wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone and reduced reflexes. Upper motor neuron signs are pyramidal weakness, drift, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Hoffmann's sign and upgoing plantars.
Know the key root values: shoulder abduction C5; elbow flexion, biceps and brachioradialis C5 to C6; wrist extension C6 to C7; triceps C7 to C8; finger flexion C8; small hand muscles T1.

Radicular pain to the thumb with C5 to C6 weakness and reduced reflexes, reproduced by neck extension, is cervical radiculopathy. Always look for upper motor neuron signs and ask about clumsy hands, gait and bladder to exclude myelopathy.
Episodic weakness only on exertion, with pain and a fixed lower motor neuron deficit, is not a TIA. Still name stroke symptoms and 000 in the safety netting.

Most cervical radiculopathy settles with analgesia, physiotherapy and modified activity. An objective motor deficit with concordant MRI warrants spinal surgical referral, and progressive weakness or myelopathy needs urgent assessment.
